newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fall in U.S. wheat price raises EU refund hopes.
newsitem.headline: Fall in U.S. wheat price raises EU refund hopes.

text.p: Further declines in U.S. wheat prices on Wednesday, following Tuesday's late plunge, rekindled chances of a higher European Union export refund this week.
But exporters' calls for a big subsidy push to foil competition from Argentina are likely to fall on deaf ears, EU member country officials and industry sources said on Thursday.

Wheat closed three to eight cents a bushel lower in Chicago and was indicated a little lower still in overnight electronic trading. Chicago December soft red wheat ended Wednesday's official session down 7-1/4 cents at 417-1/4 cents -- pegging November fob Gulf wheat near an estimated $164.40 per tonne.

Wednesday's fall, triggered by light exports and extending a sell-off on Tuesday when the U.S. reported normal seedings, left U.S. wheat about $5 per tonne cheaper than a week ago on the world market.
"Wheat was still reeling from the report that 73 percent of winter wheat has been seeded -- around average for the time of year," London-based commodity brokers GNI said on Thursday.
The EU therefore has room to raise its maximum weekly refund at the regular export tender on Thursday, traders said.
Facing U.S. criticism over wheat export subsidies, the EU has said it will try to match -- but not undercut -- U.S. wheat prices when handing out refunds.
"You're looking at about eight Ecus (per tonne)," one EU industry source calculated, adding there was no indication of what the EU Commission would actually do.
A refund of eight Ecus per tonne would price French export wheat at roughly $164 per tonne for November, traders said.
Pulling in the opposite direction was a half-percent rise in the dollar against other currencies in the past week, officials said. A stronger dollar sets the tone for lower EU refunds.

Exporters signalled on the eve of the tender, however, that they would press for more aid. They want Brussels to put up a tough response to cheap Argentine supplies, which are worth closer to $145 per tonne, ahead of harvest.
"The United States forced the EU to follow the U.S. market. But this cannot work," one exporter said on Wednesday.
But EU sources said the Commission was unlikely to heed the call. "This is not the message we want to hear," said one.
The Commission has said internal prices are still too high, despite recent price falls, and the EU is committed to the lowest possible refunds while also seeking to export.
A new sale of French wheat to Algeria at about $160 per tonne fob, excluding special costs, was likely to seem "cheap" to the Commission for the time being, one source said.
But the recent sale of French wheat to Egypt at between $164 and $167 fob now had a better chance of being covered as long as U.S. prices remained near current levels.

Last week the EU granted a maximum export refund of 6.49 Ecus per tonne for nearly 200,000 tonnes of wheat. The move valued French supplies at about $170 per tonne. An identical refund would this week be worth closer to $166 per tonne.
